Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders

somatic symptom disorder · illness anxiety · functional neurologic symptoms · factitious disorder · malingeringIs the symptom present, feared, or produced on purpose, and for what reward?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Distressing symptom outsized thoughts, worry or time somatic symptom disorder; typically over 6 months; real disease can coexist
  • Feared, little or nothing felt illness anxiety (6 months or more); made on purpose factitious (no obvious reward) or malingering (external reward)
  • Scheduled brief visits limit testing CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy); an SSRI or SNRI (selective serotonin or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) also helps
What it is

1 or more symptoms that distress or disrupt daily life an outsized response to them

Symptomatic state lasts, typically over 6 months, even if no single symptom is constant

Driver

The response, not the symptom: thoughts, anxiety or time out of proportion

Symptoms may or may not have a medical explanation

Chain

Distressing symptom outsized worry and time more health care use, many clinicians

Unneeded testing can keep care focused on the symptom

Outcome: more disability, iatrogenic harm and suicidality

Insights

A medical diagnosis does not exclude it judge the response, not whether the symptom is explained

Deception separates factitious disorder and malingering from it then the reward separates those two

The related disorders, side by sidesymptom, intent and reward
Somatic symptom1 or more distressing symptoms; excess thoughts, anxiety or timenot deceiving
Illness anxietyPreoccupied with having or getting a serious illness; symptoms absent or mildchecks the body again and again, or avoids care
Functional neurological (conversion)Altered voluntary movement or sensationfindings do not fit recognized neurologic disease
FactitiousFalsifies or induces illness, in self or in someone else (typically a child, a dependent adult or a pet)deception even with no obvious external reward
MalingeringFakes or greatly exaggerates symptomsfor an external incentive
2Urgent risks
SuicideSomatic symptom disorder carries higher rates of suicidality and disability
TestingIatrogenic harm from tests and procedures that are not needed

If the workup for the same concern is already negative, choose limiting further evaluation.

Coexisting diseaseThe diagnosis does not rule out a concurrent medical condition
Symptoms may or may not be medically explained
Another personA caregiver falsifies or induces illness in a child, dependent adult or pet
Factitious disorder imposed on another; no obvious external reward

If a caregiver's deception has injured a child, choose contacting child protective services.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Somatic symptom disorderDistressing symptom with outsized worry and time spent on itTypically over 6 months; the distressing symptom itself is the focus; not deceiving
Illness anxiety disorderFear of having or getting a serious illness; body checking or avoiding care6 months or more; symptoms absent or only mild
Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder)Change in voluntary movement or sensation, such as weaknessFindings incompatible with neurologic disease (Hoover sign); not produced on purpose
Factitious disorderFalsified or self-induced illnessDeception about one's own illness; no obvious external reward
MalingeringFaked or exaggerated symptomsAn external incentive
Factitious disorder imposed on another Former namesEarlier called factitious disorder by proxy, or Munchausen syndrome by proxyA caregiver falsifies or induces illness in a dependentThe caregiver deceives; no obvious external reward
A false belief about a bodily function1 month or more; fixed belief about the body (deformity, odor, parasite) that clear evidence does not change
Recurrent unexpected attacks1 month or more of worry about more attacks or a behavior change; fear typically acute and episodic
Pain or difficulty with attempted vaginal penetration6 months or more; no wider preoccupation or repeated care seeking
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toWhy
Distressing symptom; hours a day on it; many clinicians for the same concernSomatic symptom disorderThe response to a real, distressing symptom is out of proportion
Fears a serious disease; no or mild symptoms; checks the body oftenIllness anxiety disorderThe fear, not a symptom, is the problem
Heel of the weak leg presses down as the other leg lifts against resistanceFunctional neurological symptom disorderFindings incompatible with neurologic disease (Hoover sign); not produced on purpose
Self-induced wound; no claim or lawsuitFactitious disorderDeception with no obvious external reward, so not malingering
A clear external gain at stakeMalingeringDeception to obtain an external incentive

Pause point. The bait: one more scan or referral after the workup for the same concern is already negative, or malingering offered when no external reward exists. Further testing can feed the cycle; deception with no obvious reward is factitious disorder.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: somatic symptom disorder Symptom – 1 or more that distress or disrupt daily life · Response – thoughts about seriousness out of proportion, persistently high health anxiety, or excess time and energy on symptoms · Duration – symptomatic state persistent, typically over 6 months; any one symptom may come and go · Cause – may or may not be medically explained; a medical diagnosis does not exclude it
Defining criteria: illness anxiety disorder Fear – preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness · Symptoms – absent, or only mild · Behavior – excess health behaviors, such as body checking, or avoidance, such as of doctors and hospitals · Duration – 6 months or more
Defining criteria: functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) Symptom – 1 or more changes in voluntary motor or sensory function · Exam – findings incompatible with recognized neurologic or medical disease, such as the Hoover sign
7Treatment

Somatic symptom disorder

1

Every patientonce the diagnosis is made

Regular, brief scheduled visits

Booked on a schedule, not prompted by each new symptom.

2

Alongsideworkup for the concern already negative

Limit further evaluation

Unneeded tests and procedures can keep care focused on the symptom.

3

Psychotherapystrongest evidence

CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy)

The psychotherapy with the best evidence base.

4

Medicationbetter than placebo

An SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor)

Both classes improved symptoms compared with placebo.

Practice
  1. 38-year-old woman with 18 months of back and joint pain six specialists and normal imaging; spends hours a day researching causes has stopped working; sure something serious is missed T 36.7 °C · examination normal · blood count and inflammatory markers normal → Somatic symptom disorder → a distressing symptom with excessive thoughts and time devoted to it, persistent over 6 months; illness anxiety has no or only mild symptoms, and nothing here is feigned for a reward
  2. 29-year-old man sure he has a fatal nerve disease after a friend's diagnosis no weakness; checks his grip strength many times a day worry present for 8 months examination normal · BP 122/78 mm Hg · electromyography normal → Illness anxiety disorder → preoccupation with having a serious illness for at least 6 months with no or mild symptoms and repeated body checking; somatic symptom disorder needs a distressing symptom
  3. 24-year-old woman cannot move her left leg since an argument today pushing down with the left heel when she lifts the right leg against resistance reflexes normal and symmetric · toes downgoing · brain MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) normal · T 36.8 °C → Functional neurologic symptom disorder → weakness incompatible with neurologic disease: the left heel presses down when the right leg lifts (Hoover sign); normal reflexes and MRI argue against a stroke, and nothing suggests deliberate falsification
  4. 33-year-old woman, a pharmacy technician, with a thigh wound that keeps reopening cultures grow different stool organisms each time a syringe found in her bag; no lawsuit or disability claim T 38.2 °C · leukocytes 13,000/mm³ → Factitious disorder → deliberate induction of disease with deception and no obvious external reward; malingering needs an external incentive, and patients with somatic symptom disorder are not trying to deceive
  5. 45-year-old man in police custody asks for oxycodone for back pain pain started at the arrest; limps only when watched court date next week straight-leg raise negative seated and supine · strength and reflexes normal · BP 130/84 mm Hg → Malingering → symptoms overstated to obtain external incentives; factitious disorder deceives without an obvious external reward
  6. 4-year-old boy with a 2nd admission this year for blood in his urine bleeding seen only by his mother; no custody or benefit claim repeated urinalyses normal when nurses collect them T 36.9 °C · BP 96/60 mm Hg · creatinine normal → Factitious disorder imposed on another (mother) → a caregiver falsifies illness in a child without external incentives; the findings exist only in her reports and vanish under observation
  7. 36-year-old woman with abdominal pain for 3 years 11 emergency visits this year, all workups negative; fears a missed cancer asks for another computed tomography scan examination unchanged · BP 118/76 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal → Regular scheduled brief visits → regular, time-limited appointments rather than symptom-driven visits; limit further evaluation, since unnecessary testing can perpetuate symptom-focused health care use; CBT and an SSRI or SNRI can help
Pairs with Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: is the fear about attacks, or about having a disease?
Transferable rule

Ask two questions before naming it: is the symptom produced on purpose, and is there an external reward?
